How long do you stay on one screen before switching? In 2004 it was about 2.5 minutes. Guess first 👀

Researcher Gloria Mark has timed how long people stay on one screen before switching. In 2004: about two and a half minutes. In her studies from 2016 to 2020: 47 seconds, on average.

Why it matters: every switch costs a little focus, and 47-second hops add up to a day that felt busy but didn't get far.

Do this: for your next task, go full screen. One window, nothing else, until it's done.

new.caption:
Everything takes longer than you think? It's not just you. You're not bad at planning. Everyone is.

THE STUDY: students guessed their thesis would take 34 days on average. It took 56. Even their worst-case guess, 49 days, was too short. Only about 3 in 10 finished in the time they predicted. It's called the planning fallacy.

WHY IT HAPPENS: when we plan, we picture the day where everything goes right: no sick kid, no slow reply, no file that won't open. And we quietly ignore how long the last one actually took.

THE FIRST FIX:
1. Before you guess, ask "how long did this take LAST time?", not "how long should it take?"
2. Look it up if you can: your calendar, old emails, the last report's date.
3. Then add half again. Think 2 hours? Plan 3. Think a week? Plan a week and a half.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, your plan looks worse on paper. Week 1, you finish when you said you would, maybe for the first time in a while. Month 1, people start trusting your "by Friday".

The rule that stays: plan from your past, not your hopes.

Do this: today, add half again to your next time guess.

Send this to the friend who says "it'll be quick." Part 2 tonight at 7: break it into steps, the fix that's backed by research.

new.caption:
"It'll take an hour." It won't. Here's the fix that's backed by research.

THE RESEARCH: in a study, people who listed every step of a task before guessing how long it would take made longer, more realistic guesses. Hidden steps are where the time goes. It works best for tasks with lots of parts.

HOW TO DO IT ("update the website", unpacked):
1. Find the old photos (15 min)
2. Wait for the new ones from Sam (1 day of waiting, 5 min of asking)
3. Write the new text (45 min)
4. Send it for a check, then fix the comments (30 min + a day)
5. Upload and test on your phone (20 min)
"An hour" was really about 2 hours of work and 2 days of waiting. (The website task is made up for this post.)

THE HIDDEN STEPS TO ALWAYS ADD: waiting for someone, setup (logins, finding files), the back-and-forth, travel, and the check at the end.

WITH THIS MORNING'S FIX: compare your total with how long it took last time, and if they disagree, trust last time.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, Monday's plan fits inside Monday. Week 1, fewer 9 pm "how is this not done?" moments. Month 1, your estimates become the ones people plan around.

The rule that stays: guess the steps, not the task.

Do this: tonight, take Monday's biggest task, write down its steps, then guess the time.

Send this to your Monday planner friend. Part 2 of 2.

new.caption:
Monday isn't magic. It's a handle. Grab it tonight.

THE RESEARCH: researchers looked at the gym records of about 12,000 students at one US university. At the start of a new week, the chance of a gym visit was 33.4% higher than usual. The start of a month: 14.4%. The start of a semester: 47.1%. They call it the fresh start effect: a new week feels like a clean page, so people try again.

THE HONEST PART: it's correlational. It shows when people start, not that Mondays make anything work. And it cuts both ways: waiting for Monday can turn into waiting forever.

HOW TO USE IT:
1. Tonight, pick one thing you want to start.
2. Write when and where: "Monday, 8 am, after coffee."
3. Missed it? Every day has a handle: tomorrow morning, after lunch, the next hour.

Do this: tonight, pick one thing and write when you'll start it: "Monday, 8 am, after coffee."

Send this to the friend waiting for a fresh start.

new.caption:
Inbox open all day again? Today's word: Batch.

One Word No. 2 (No. 1 was "Later"). Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

THE RESEARCH: in a 2-week study, people who checked email only 3 times a day felt less stressed than when they could check as often as they liked.

HOW TO BATCH:
1. Pick 3 times: say 9:30, 1:00 and 4:30.
2. Close the email tab (and turn off email notifications) between them.
3. At each check: reply, file or schedule. Nothing stays "unread to deal with later".
4. Worried about missing something urgent? Tell people to call or text for urgent things.

THE CATCH: if your job is answering email (support, dispatch), batch something else, like chat or news.

Do this: tomorrow, write your 3 check times on a sticky note and close the tab.

One Word No. 3 is Wednesday at 5 pm.
